Comparing love of God (c) with love of that creature (b): by intensity c need exceed b only finitely, or not at all; by the greatness of the good willed it exceeds infinitely; by firmness it need not exceed, since love of self is naturally firmest in this life; by preference it exceeds infinitely, since no one should give up love of God for anything.
claims: Christ's humanity is the creature to be willed the greatest good.
Love of God exceeds love of creatures infinitely in good willed and in preference, but not necessarily in intensity.

rh-l1q3-d1e6183.summary: On intensity, the conclusion is granted: one need not love God more intensely than a creature in this life, and may love God as remissly as one likes provided one wills him the highest honor. As to the good willed, the precept requires that love of God be for his own sake and love of creatures for another, circumstances that differ in species, so no multiplication of the latter reaches the former. Christ's humanity is to be loved above all creatures as to the good willed.
claims: One need not love God more intensely than a creature.
Love of God for his own sake differs in species from love of creatures for another.

rh-l1q3-d1e6232.summary: Reply to the sixth principal argument. In 'enjoyment is to be enjoyed' the ablative can express object or formal cause. As object it is false of created enjoyment, which is loved for God; as formal cause it is true but the inference fails. From 'I love enjoyment by enjoyment' it does not follow that I enjoy enjoyment, as 'I love God by use' does not imply using God. By one and the same love I enjoy God and use my enjoyment, so one love is enjoyment and use with respect to different objects.
claims: The same act can be enjoyment of God and use of itself.
'Enjoyment is to be enjoyed' is ambiguous between object and formal cause.

rh-l1q3-d1e6284.summary: Reply to the confirmations. One should love God more than one's act of enjoyment, but it does not follow that one is bound to love God more than to enjoy God. Socrates is bound to love a more than b, but it does not follow that he should rather will whatever opposes b than what opposes a, since some things, like hatred of God, oppose both. If enjoyment is loved by another act there is no infinite regress: some love is not loved by a distinct act, and after three or four reflexive acts awareness of the first fades, owing to the finitude of the cognitive power.
claims: Loving God more than one's enjoyment does not imply loving God more than enjoying God.
Reflexive acts stop after a few iterations because cognitive power is finite.

rh-l1q3-d1e6358.summary: Reply to the seventh principal argument: nothing other than God can satisfy the appetite effectively.
claims: Only God can effectively satisfy the human appetite.

rh-l1q3-d1e6367.summary: On the mind's finite capacity: if 'by' denotes final cause, the mind can be satisfied by something finite, since the light of glory, the beatific act received in the mind, is finite. If it denotes efficient cause, it cannot be satisfied by anything finite.
claims: The mind is satisfied formally by a finite act but effectively only by God.

rh-l1q3-d1e6387.summary: Objection: every finite effect can be produced by a finite cause. Reply: false, since many finite effects such as grace, the soul, and angels can be produced only by an infinite power.
claims: Some finite effects require infinite power.

rh-l1q3-d1e6401.summary: Reply to the other form: from God exceeding the mind and body being exceeded by it, it does not follow that something equal to the mind can satisfy it. Something is equal to the mind, namely itself, but that does not satisfy it.
claims: Equality to the mind does not imply power to satisfy it.

rh-l1q3-d1e6417.summary: Reply to the eighth principal argument: neither the antecedent is true nor the inference valid.

rh-l1q3-d1e6424.summary: The antecedent is false: otherwise one would be bound to love God more than God and oneself, and to love all things, including demons and animals, and God more than all. So 'Socrates must love God above all' is false literally and must be expounded as 'above all things Socrates should love', among which God is not.
claims: 'Love God above all' is literally false and must be expounded.

rh-l1q3-d1e6450.summary: The consequent is false too: one is not bound to will a thousand others in charity and oneself without rather than the reverse. In many cases one should choose what one believes less to God's honor, since God commands that one should rather will oneself in grace than a thousand others.
claims: One should prefer one's own grace to that of a thousand others.
One may be bound to choose what is less to God's honor.

rh-l1q3-d1e6472.summary: The inference also fails, its antecedent being true in a good sense and its consequent false. Reply to the ninth principal argument: given a latitude of effort, one may love God at any degree. It may be granted that one may love a creature at any degree, since the precept on the greatness of love concerns not intensity but the good willed and its circumstance, that God's due good be willed for himself. One beginning to enjoy God may love God infinitely less intensely than Plato and yet infinitely more as to the good willed.
claims: The precept concerns the good willed, not the intensity of the act.
One may love God less intensely yet infinitely more as to the good willed.

rh-l1q3-d1e6530.summary: Reply to the tenth principal argument. The precept does not necessitate sin. Later one is bound to the same thing by more causes: God requires that one will him the highest honor, owed by precept and by benefit, and asks for benefits nothing beyond what he imposes by precept. Continuous existence is a great benefit that creates new obligations, but not to love more, since one was already bound with one's whole heart.
claims: Benefits add new grounds for the same obligation, not greater obligation.

rh-l1q3-d1e6562.summary: Reply on humans and angels: a human is bound more, i.e. by more causes, but not to love more in this life, only as much as he can. In heaven a human may love God more than an angel. Objection: the angel has better natural endowments.
claims: Humans are bound by more causes, not to greater love, than angels.

rh-l1q3-d1e6580.summary: Reply: human nature will be aided more by the light of grace and God's cooperation; as the Virgin is exalted above all angels, she loves God more intensely than any of them.
claims: Grace can raise humans above angels in love.
The Virgin loves God more than any angel.

rh-l1q3-d1e6591.summary: Reply on Christ's soul: it is bound more, but Socrates could not, by sinning and being forgiven infinitely, come to owe as much as Christ's soul, since these debts are not of the same kind.
claims: Debts of love from forgiveness and from Christ's grace are not commensurable.

rh-l1q3-d1e6609.summary: Reply to the eleventh principal argument. If 'more' concerns the good willed or the circumstance of willing, one is not bound to love oneself more than God. Aristotle's dictum is true as to knowledge, not as to the greatness of what is willed.
claims: One is not bound to love oneself more than God as to the good willed.
Aristotle's priority of self-love concerns knowledge.

rh-l1q3-d1e6631.summary: Objection: is a saint bound to love God more than a newborn? Not by intensity, nor by greater good willed, nor by circumstance; none of these can be said.
claims: No sense of 'more' fits a saint's greater obligation.

rh-l1q3-d1e6644.summary: Reply: 'Socrates is bound to love God more than Plato is' is amphibolous, since 'more' can modify 'bound' (true: by more causes) or 'love' (false: one is bound to love equally).
claims: 'Bound to love more' is amphibolous between more grounds and more love.

rh-l1q3-d1e6665.summary: Reply to the annihilation argument: yes, one should prefer annihilation to mortal sin.
claims: One should prefer annihilation to mortal sin.

rh-l1q3-d1e6674.summary: Reply to the twelfth principal argument: one is not bound equally before and after redemption; and we should not love Christ's humanity more than God.
claims: Redemption increases the grounds of obligation.
Christ's humanity is not to be loved more than God.

rh-l1q3-d1e6685.summary: Reply to the thirteenth: the conclusion is granted.
claims: One can meritoriously enjoy a creature through invincible ignorance.
